newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi says city may get an extra $936 mln.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi says city may get an extra $936 mln.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi said Thursday the city made strides in improving its finances for the current and next fiscal years, but warned there still are concerns about its long-term health.
Hevesi said in a statement he largely agreed with Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's estimate for a 1997 fiscal surplus, saying the sum should total at least $856 million.
And the city comptroller added that his office has found from $699 million to $936 million of available resources that Giuliani has not included in his budget plan for fiscal 1998.

Although the Republican mayor plans to use $656 million of the surplus to help close a 1998 budget gap, Hevesi, who spoke to the City Council, said Giuliani's plan still had risks of $1.1 billion to $1.49 billion.
The city starts its new fiscal year on July 1, and its budget director has said he expects a 1998 budget to be approved around the June 10 target date.

Hevesi projected the city's 1998 budget gap at $173 million to $796 million, assuming that proposed tax cut plan is put in place, and that the 14-percent personal income tax surcharge is extended beyond December 1997. But he said that as Giuliani has budgeted $200 million for the general reserve, and forecast a $200 million surplus for fiscal 1998, the near-term budget gaps should be manageable.
However, New York City will face yawning budget gaps later, with the fiscal 1999 gap projected at $2 billion, the gap in 2000 at $2.9 billion and the one in 2001 at $2.7 billion.

Hevesi, a Democrat who decided not to challenge Giuliani in the November mayoral election, urged him to use the 1997 -- a record when measured in dollar terms -- to shore up the city's long-term finances by retiring debt, increasing pay-as-you-go capital financing and reducing the use of one-shots.

In the next fiscal year, the Board of Education has to find $308 million in revenues and savings to balance its budget, including $30 million above what was planned for extra administrative costs that result from freeing teachers from supervising lunchrooms by using aides, Hevesi noted.
